scientific_background_evidence.display_text: Comparative magnesium studies support cautious form-level comparison, especially for citrate versus oxide, without justifying a universal best-form claim.

en.text: Comparative magnesium studies support cautious form-level comparison, especially for citrate versus oxide, without justifying a universal best-form claim.
The clearest direct comparison is citrate versus oxide, and later reviews continue to treat oxide as less bioavailable while keeping comparison language cautious.
When a label discloses citrate or oxide, that form detail is more useful for comparison than a broad magnesium headline alone.
Do not generalize citrate-versus-oxide findings to every magnesium form or every formula setting.

scientific_background_evidence.variant_label: Magnesium citrate versus oxide comparison context
scientific_background_evidence.display_text: Human comparison studies consistently support magnesium citrate as more bioavailable than oxide, but this should stay a form-comparison signal rather than a blanket ranking rule.

en.text: Human comparison studies consistently support magnesium citrate as more bioavailable than oxide, but this should stay a form-comparison signal rather than a blanket ranking rule.
Randomized human work found greater urinary and serum magnesium response with citrate than oxide, and later review-level summaries align with that direction.
If two labels disclose citrate versus oxide, the form difference is meaningful enough to treat them as different comparison lanes.
This comparison does not prove that every citrate product is better than every oxide product in every dose or blended formula.

scientific_background_evidence.display_text: For magnesium products, exact form disclosure carries more comparison value than a generic magnesium headline, and citrate-versus-oxide literature is most useful as a label-reading aid.

en.text: For magnesium products, exact form disclosure carries more comparison value than a generic magnesium headline, and citrate-versus-oxide literature is most useful as a label-reading aid.
Direct absorption evidence helps compare disclosed forms, but it does not remove the need to check elemental amount and formula context.
Check the disclosed form and the labeled magnesium amount before assuming two products belong in the same comparison set.
A better-absorbed form on paper does not make every disclosed product interchangeable or universally preferable.

scientific_background_evidence.display_text: Human studies support cautious comparison between ferrous bisglycinate and ferrous sulfate, especially when labels disclose the exact form and elemental dose, without turning that into a universal best-form claim.

en.text: Human studies support cautious comparison between ferrous bisglycinate and ferrous sulfate, especially when labels disclose the exact form and elemental dose, without turning that into a universal best-form claim.

Randomized and human absorption studies make ferrous bisglycinate versus ferrous sulfate a real comparison lane, but the evidence is more useful for careful label interpretation than for one-line superiority claims.
If the label specifies ferrous bisglycinate or ferrous sulfate, that form disclosure is worth checking before comparing dose or tolerability expectations.
Lower-dose bisglycinate results should not be converted into a blanket better-for-everyone claim across all doses and populations.

scientific_background_evidence.display_text: Ferrous bisglycinate has enough human comparison evidence to support a specific form-aware narrative against ferrous sulfate, especially around lower-dose comparison, but not a universal superiority ranking.

en.text: Ferrous bisglycinate has enough human comparison evidence to support a specific form-aware narrative against ferrous sulfate, especially around lower-dose comparison, but not a universal superiority ranking.
Human trials comparing 18 to 25 mg ferrous bisglycinate against higher-dose ferrous sulfate make this a meaningful form-comparison lane, but context still matters.
When the label clearly says ferrous bisglycinate, compare it against dose, co-ingredients, and sulfate-based products instead of treating all oral iron forms as interchangeable.
This evidence supports a cautious comparison lane, not a rule that every bisglycinate formula will outperform every sulfate formula.

en.text: For iron supplements, exact form disclosure and elemental dose carry more comparison value than a generic iron headline, and bisglycinate-versus-sulfate studies are most useful as a label-reading boundary.
Dose and exact oral form still shape interpretation, even when comparative studies make one form-comparison lane more evidence-rich than another.
Check the labeled form, elemental iron amount, and whether the product is a simple single-form iron or a broader blend before comparing products.
One studied form difference does not remove the need to read dose, population setting, and formula complexity carefully.
